title: Natural selection makes organisms simpler and more engineering-like

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Natural selection makes organisms simpler and more engineering-like

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Rather than generating complexity, the main effect of natural selection is to make biological systems avoid complexity, favoring simple, somewhat independent components with smoothly adjustable properties, as in engineered systems.

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: my strong suspicion is that in fact the main effect of natural selection is almost exactly the opposite: it tends to make biological systems avoid complexity, and be more like systems in engineering.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 8, “Implications for Everyday Systems”; section “Fundamental Issues in Biology” (from p. 383), p. 393. Scope: biological organisms under natural selection

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch08-15: needs-new-data, resolvability 0.32

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Some experimental evolution datasets permit local tests, but they do not represent organismal history or the main effect of natural selection generally. The necessary before-and-after causal records and standardized architecture measures are largely missing. A broad resolution requires new comparative and experimental data.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Compare trait complexity, modular independence, and smooth parameter sensitivity before and after known episodes or experiments of strong selection, controlling for drift and developmental constraint. Consistent increases in modular simplicity attributable to selection would support the claim, while selection-driven complexity increases would refute it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Engineering-like and complexity are multidimensional judgments.

Historical selection intensity is rarely observed directly.

Developmental constraints can mimic selection for modularity.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
discriminating power: 0.25
operationalizability: 0.3
analysis feasibility: 0.32
data existence: 0.48
data adequacy: 0.2

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Modularity and the smoothness of quantitative traits can be measured in model organisms, which gives a partial test. The main effect of selection is a global causal claim, and public datasets do not separate selection's effect from developmental constraints that produce simple parts for other reasons. Discriminating power stays low.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Measure modularity, independence of parts, and smoothness of trait variation for characters ranked by evidence of selection. A positive association between selection and those engineering-like properties would support the claim; complex, tightly coupled traits under strong selection would count against it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Like systems in engineering is a metaphor until modularity and smooth adjustability are defined.

Selection is often inferred from the same simplicity the claim treats as its effect.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
